120.title: The luminous mysteries
120.hook: added by John Paul II in 2002: baptism, Cana, the kingdom, transfiguration, Eucharist (Thursdays)
120.howItsDone: Catholics who use them pray the luminous mysteries of the rosary on Thursdays, meditating on the Baptism of Jesus, the Wedding at Cana, the Proclamation of the Kingdom, the Transfiguration and the Institution of the Eucharist; some keep the traditional fifteen mysteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the joyful mysteries, and the word mystery: a hidden thing opened up. Your line was joy has a story.

Picture the whole Gospel laid out on a table, and the rosary's mysteries as pins stuck into it. For a long time there were fifteen. Five joyful: the birth and childhood of Jesus. Five sorrowful: his suffering and death. Five glorious: the resurrection and after. There's a big empty stretch in the middle. Jesus is twelve in the Temple, and the very next pin is the night before he dies. Everything in between, the baptism, the miracles, the parables, the crowds, is missing. Then in October 2002, a pope who had prayed the rosary since he was young added five.
screen: `FIFTEEN MYSTERIES.` → `A GAP IN THE MIDDLE.` → `2002: A POPE ADDS FIVE.`

segments.voice: Pope John Paul the Second called them the mysteries of light, in Latin mysteria lucis. Luminous means full of light. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." These five cover his public life, when that light was out in the open. First, the Baptism in the Jordan: Jesus goes down into the water, the heavens open, and a voice calls him the beloved Son. Second, the Wedding at Cana: the wine runs out, and Mary tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Water becomes wine, his first sign. Third, the Proclamation of the Kingdom: the preaching, the call to turn around, the forgiveness. Fourth, the Transfiguration: on a mountain, his face shines like the sun in front of three friends. Fifth, the Institution of the Eucharist: the Last Supper, the bread and cup you met at the consecration last week. The baptism, Cana and the mountain were all stories in Camp Two; now they're beads. The Pope suggested praying them on Thursdays, the day of the Last Supper, and moved the joyful mysteries to Saturday to make room. He said plainly the addition was offered freely, not imposed. Some Catholics pray all twenty. Some keep the traditional fifteen. Both are at home in the Church. The gap is filled: the rosary now walks through the whole life, including the years when the light was out on the road.
screen: `MYSTERIA LUCIS: MYSTERIES OF LIGHT.` · `JORDAN, CANA, THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MOUNTAIN, THE SUPPER.` · `OFFERED FREELY, NOT IMPOSED.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Pick one scene, the river, the wedding running out of wine, the crowds, the mountain, the supper, and put yourself inside it; at Cana, maybe you're a servant, told to fill jars with water and not sure why. If you pray, begin a luminous decade on your fingers, and let the scene play. If you don't, stay with the picture, and notice where the light falls.
Luminous mysteries. Five scenes of light from Jesus's public life, added to the rosary in 2002 and prayed on Thursdays. Today's word.

121.title: The sorrowful mysteries
121.hook: the agony, the scourging, the thorns, the carrying, the cross (Tuesdays and Fridays)
121.carry: walk the hard road with him
121.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the sorrowful mysteries on Tuesdays and Fridays, and some through Lent, offering a decade for someone who is suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luminous mysteries: the baptism, Cana, the kingdom, the Transfiguration, the Last Supper. Your line was the light years.

A diagnosis. A funeral. A night in a hospital corridor with bad coffee. When someone is living through a week like that, there's often nothing anyone can fix. What's left is to stay, and walk next to them for a while. On Tuesdays and Fridays, Catholics who pray the rosary do something like that with Jesus. They take the beads and walk through the last night and day of his life, one decade at a time. Five scenes, none of them easy.
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.` → `NOTHING TO FIX. STAY.` → `TUESDAYS AND FRIDAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the agony in the garden. The night before he dies, Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and Luke says his sweat fell like drops of blood. In the Douay-Rheims Bible his prayer is this: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Second, the scourging at the pillar: the Roman soldiers whip him. Third, the crowning with thorns: they twist a crown out of thorns, throw a purple cloak on him, and mock him as a king. Fourth, the carrying of the cross, through the streets, with a stranger named Simon of Cyrene pressed into helping. Fifth, the crucifixion: darkness over the land at midday, and death. Notice the word agony. In Luke's Greek it's agonia, a word Greeks also used for the strain of a contest: a struggle, not only pain. Why would anyone choose to pray through this, twice a week? Catholics give a few answers. One: love stays. Mary stood by the cross, and praying these mysteries is a way of standing there too. Two: the sorrowful mysteries are for people who are suffering. Someone in chemo, someone grieving, someone in prison can find their own night in his. Some Catholics offer a sorrowful decade for a particular person who is hurting. Three: they don't end here. The rosary never leaves him in the tomb; tomorrow comes the glory. And one practical note: in his 2002 letter on the rosary, Pope John Paul the Second suggested the sorrowful mysteries for Tuesdays and Fridays, and some also pray them on the Sundays of Lent.

Rest your eyes, open and soft, on one spot, picture the night, the olive trees, the friends asleep, and keep watch; when your mind drifts, come back, the way you'd come back to a friend. If you pray the rosary, you can pray a sorrowful decade here; if you don't, just keep watch.

122.title: The glorious mysteries
122.hook: resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, assumption, Mary crowned (Wednesdays and Sundays)
122.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the glorious mysteries on Wednesdays and Sundays, moving from the empty tomb to Mary crowned in heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sorrowful mysteries: the garden, the pillar, the thorns, the cross carried, the cross. Your line was walk the hard road with him.

Some people read the last page of a novel first. They want to know it ends all right before they can bear the middle. The rosary, in a way, lets you do that. Yesterday's beads left Jesus on the cross, then in the tomb. If they stopped there, it would be a prayer of grief. They don't. On Wednesdays and Sundays, Catholics pick up the beads and pray the last page: five scenes of what happens after.
screen: `READ THE LAST PAGE FIRST.` → `THE BEADS DON'T STOP AT THE TOMB.` → `WEDNESDAYS AND SUNDAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the resurrection. Women come to the tomb at dawn with spices, and it's empty. In the Douay-Rheims, the angels tell them, "He is not here, but is risen." Second, the ascension: forty days later, Jesus is taken up out of the disciples' sight. Third, the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost: wind, tongues like fire, and frightened people suddenly speaking in the street. Those three are all in the Bible. The last two are about Mary, and here it's honest to say where they come from. The fourth is the assumption: Catholics believe that at the end of her life Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heaven. The Bible doesn't describe this. It's an old tradition, celebrated for centuries, and Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it as Catholic teaching in 1950. The Orthodox keep a closely related feast called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, and most Protestant churches don't hold the teaching. The fifth is the coronation: Mary crowned as queen of heaven. Catholics often picture it through the book of Revelation, which the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." So what's the point of the five together? The Greek word for glory is doxa, splendor, and behind it in the Bible stands the Hebrew kavod, which also means weight. Glory shines, and it's heavy. The glorious mysteries say the story ends heavy with light. What happened to Jesus, Catholics say, is meant to happen to everyone: risen, taken home, crowned. Mary goes first, as the first disciple. The end is glory, and the hard road leads there.
screen: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.` · `THE ASCENSION AND PENTECOST.` · `MARY TAKEN UP, MARY CROWNED.` · `DOXA: GLORY, WEIGHT AND LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENDS HEAVY WITH LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Choose the first one, the empty tomb at dawn: picture the light coming up, and the women running back with the news. Then think of one thing in your own life that felt finished and wasn't, a friendship that came back, a hope that returned. If you pray the rosary, pray the decade here; if you don't, just stay with the dawn.
Glorious mysteries. Resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, the assumption, Mary crowned. The last page, read on Wednesdays and Sundays. Today's word.

123.title: Hail, Holy Queen
123.hook: the closing prayer calls us poor banished children, sighing in this valley of tears
123.carry: our life, our sweetness, our hope
123.howItsDone: Catholics often close the rosary with the Salve Regina, and monasteries and religious communities sing it, often in Latin, at night prayer, the last prayer of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the glorious mysteries, the last page of the rosary. Your line was the end is glory.

Poor banished children of Eve. Mourning and weeping, in this valley of tears. Those lines come from a prayer that monks and nuns sing at the end of the day. The last service is over, the lights are going down, and they turn toward an image of Mary and sing it slowly, in Latin, before the great silence of the night. When Catholics finish the five decades of a rosary, they often close with the same prayer. It doesn't pretend life is easy.
screen: `A VALLEY OF TEARS.` → `ONE MORE SONG BEFORE SILENCE.` → `THE END OF A ROSARY.`

segments.voice: Salve Regina is Latin for Hail, Queen. It opens like this: "Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae, vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve." In the traditional English form Catholics say it this way: "Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears." Look at who's speaking. Not the happy and settled. Exiles. Children of Eve, which means everyone, far from home. The prayer takes the Garden of Eden story seriously: in its picture, people are not where they were made to be. And it doesn't cover the ache with a smile. Mourning and weeping, it says. Then it turns. It asks Mary, called our advocate, to turn her eyes of mercy toward us, and after this exile, to show us Jesus. That's the shape: honest about the valley, and hopeful about the way out. It comes from the monasteries of medieval Europe. It's often credited to a monk named Hermann of Reichenau, remembered as so disabled he could barely move or speak, and as a writer on music and astronomy anyway. But the attribution isn't certain, and other names have been suggested. A pious story says Bernard of Clairvaux added the three cries at the end, O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary; that's a legend, not a record. What's clear is that it traveled: into night prayer in monasteries, and onto the end of the rosary.
screen: `SALVE, REGINA: HAIL, QUEEN.` · `POOR BANISHED CHILDREN OF EVE.` · `HONEST ABOUT THE VALLEY.` · `AN OLD PRAYER, AUTHOR UNSURE.` · then, large: `OUR LIFE, OUR SWEETNESS AND OUR HOPE.`

segments.voice: Think of something that feels like your own valley right now, the thing you'd sigh about if someone asked, and don't tidy it up. Then, if you pray, say the first line slowly: Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope; if you know the rest, go on. If you don't pray, just notice the order: first the honest sigh, then the hope.
Salve Regina. Hail, Queen. The old closing prayer of the rosary and of the monastery night, honest about the valley of tears. Today's word.

124.title: One decade a day
124.hook: a whole rosary takes about twenty minutes; a single decade is a real prayer too
124.howItsDone: Some Catholics who can't pray a full rosary pray a single decade each day, often while walking, driving or waiting, sometimes on a one-decade ring or pocket chaplet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salve Regina, the old prayer that closes the rosary. Your line was our life, our sweetness, our hope.

Meant to pray the rosary. Didn't. Plenty of people with beads in a drawer could say that. A whole rosary, five decades with the opening and closing prayers, takes about twenty minutes. That's a long time on a Tuesday with a sick kid and an inbox. So it slides, and then it slides for a month, and the beads sit in a drawer looking at you. Today is small on purpose: what happens if, instead of twenty minutes, you give it four? One decade a day.
screen: `TWENTY MINUTES ON A TUESDAY.` → `THE BEADS IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE FOUR?`

segments.voice: Start with the word bead. In Old English, the word gebed meant a prayer. People counted prayers on strings of small balls, and over time the name of the prayer slid over onto the thing you counted it on. A bead was a prayer before it was a bead. Now the decade: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be, with one mystery held in mind. At a normal pace it takes three or four minutes. Is that a real prayer, or a cut-down one? The rosary isn't a single block that only counts if you finish it. It's built from decades, and each one stands on its own, with its own beginning and end: an Our Father, the Hail Marys, a Glory Be. Some Catholics pray a decade on the drive to work, walking the dog, or waiting for the kettle. Some carry a single decade ring or a small one-decade chaplet in a pocket. The arithmetic is simple. Seven decades in a week is more than one whole rosary. And a decade fits inside a Tuesday. That's the whole week on the rosary: how it's built, the joyful, luminous, sorrowful and glorious mysteries, the Salve Regina, and now this. Ten beads is enough to begin.

segments.voice: Rest one hand open, and with each slow breath fold down one finger: ten breaths, ten fingers, the feel of a decade. If you pray the rosary, say a Hail Mary on each one instead, with one mystery in mind. If you don't, just count the breaths and notice how short ten really is.
Decade. One Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be, said in three or four minutes, a real prayer on its own. Today's word.

125.title: What a sacrament is
125.hook: an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies (CCC 1131)
125.howItsDone: Catholics receive the seven sacraments at key moments of life, from baptism as a baby to anointing when seriously ill, with the Eucharist and confession received again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one decade a day, the end of the rosary week. Your line was ten beads is enough.

Most signs just point. A road sign says the bridge is ahead; it doesn't build the bridge. But a few signs do what they say. A referee blows the whistle, and the game stops. A judge says you're married, and you are. Someone says I'm sorry, and something between you really shifts. The words and the gesture don't just describe a thing; they make it happen. Catholics believe God works like that in seven particular moments of a life. Today, the word for them: sacrament.
screen: `MOST SIGNS JUST POINT.` → `SOME SIGNS DO WHAT THEY SAY.` → `SEVEN MOMENTS.`

segments.voice: The word comes from Latin, sacramentum. In ancient Rome it meant an oath, the solemn vow a soldier swore when he joined the army, something that bound his whole life. Early Latin Christians used it to translate mysterion, the Greek word behind the rosary's mysteries last week. So a sacrament is both: a promise that binds, and a mystery you can't fully see into. The Catechism of the Catholic Church, in paragraph 1131, puts it this way: sacraments are signs that actually give grace, set up by Christ and entrusted to the Church, through which God's own life is shared with us. Older catechisms say it shorter: an outward sign that gives the grace it signifies. Water that washes. Oil that strengthens. Bread that feeds. The sign isn't a picture of something happening elsewhere; Catholics believe it's where the thing happens. And it doesn't depend on the priest being a saint that morning: the Church teaches that Christ is the one acting. There are seven. Baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist bring you in. Reconciliation and the anointing of the sick heal. Holy orders and matrimony set a life toward serving others. The Council of Trent confirmed the list of seven. Christians count differently here. The Orthodox also speak of holy mysteries, and usually list the same seven. Lutheran and Reformed churches generally name two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Some communities, like the Quakers, keep no outward sacraments at all. Over the next week, i'll take the seven one at a time.
screen: `SACRAMENTUM: A SOLDIER'S OATH.` · `MYSTERION: A MYSTERY.` · `A SIGN THAT GIVES WHAT IT SHOWS.` · `SEVEN: IN, HEALING, SERVICE.` · then, large: `SIGNS THAT DO SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Look at your own hands and remember one time they did more than the motion: a handshake that closed a deal, a hand on a shoulder at a funeral, a ring put on a finger. Recall it clearly, where you were and who was there, and see how a small outward thing carried something large. If you pray, give thanks for the signs in your life.
Sacrament. From the Latin for a soldier's oath: an outward sign, given by Christ, that Catholics believe gives the grace it shows. Today's word.

126.title: Baptism
126.hook: water poured three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit
126.howItsDone: Catholics are usually baptized as babies: the priest or deacon pours water over the head three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with godparents promising to help raise the child in the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacrament: a sign that does what it shows. Your line was signs that do something.

Sunday afternoon, at the back of a church. A baby in a white outfit that took three people to get onto her. Grandparents with phones up. A godmother holding a candle a little too close to her hair. The priest takes a small shell or a jug and pours water over the baby's forehead, once, twice, three times, saying the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The baby is often furious about it. Everyone else is smiling. Catholics believe something enormous just happened, in a few seconds. The first of the seven: baptism.
screen: `A BABY IN WHITE.` → `WATER, THREE TIMES.` → `A FEW SECONDS, SOMETHING ENORMOUS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, plunge or immerse. Some churches go right under the water; others pour, and the Catholic Church allows both. Either way, the sign is washing: going under, coming up. Jesus himself was baptized by John in the Jordan. At the end of Matthew's Gospel he sends his followers out with this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." That's where the three names come from, and the three pourings follow them. The Catechism names what Catholics believe it does: sins washed away, a new birth as a child of God, membership in the Church, and a mark on the soul that can never be undone, which is why a person is baptized only once. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit. So Catholics call it a birth; some keep the date like a birthday. No baby comes alone. Godparents promise to help raise the child in the faith. In many Hispanic families they're padrinos, and the parents and godparents become compadres, family for life. In many Filipino families they're ninong and ninang, and there are often several. Two surprises. In an emergency, anyone can baptize, even someone who isn't Christian, pouring water and saying those words, intending what the Church does. And the Church recognizes other Christian churches' baptisms done with water and the same three names. Christians differ on when: Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and others baptize babies, while Baptists and others baptize only those old enough to profess faith.
